extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, mathematical expositors, teachers, and advanced students interested in proof exposition
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for composing mathematical exposition (lectures, notes, or textbook-style proofs) that make proofs feel inevitable and discoverable rather than magical. Emphasizes motivation, clarity, and showing plausible discovery paths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every step should be motivated and clear
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers need logical justification for each move.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give motivation for each step so the reader understands why it is reasonable to make that move; avoid unexplained leaps. Ensure clarity so the logical progression is evident rather than hidden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should feel they could have arrived at the results themselves
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposition should feel discoverable, not magical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure explanations so readers can imagine themselves finding the argument; present intermediate thoughts or heuristics that make the final steps feel within reach for the intended audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render ideas totally perspicuous
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for maximal perspicuity: remove obscurity, present concepts and connections so they are immediately understandable rather than merely stated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weak solution: explain why each step is reasonable
rubrics_metrics.description: A weak solution to the exposition problem explains why individual steps are reasonable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide local justifications and intuitive reasons for moves in the argument. This prevents the appearance of arbitrary or ad hoc steps but may stop short of deeper theoretical grounding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strong solution: provide theoretical justification for calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: A strong solution gives a theoretical account of why the calculation or method works, not merely that it does.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Go beyond stepwise plausibility to show underlying principles or theory that justify the approach; explain why the calculation must succeed in a broader sense, making the argument more convincing and explanatory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers should understand why problems matter before diving into technical details.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce the significance, context, or purpose of the problem early so readers appreciate the direction of the argument and are equipped to follow technical developments with an aim in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demystification: show how definitions/proofs could be discovered
rubrics_metrics.description: Address the 'exposition problem' by showing how seemingly miraculous definitions or proofs are actually discoverable by a reasonable mathematician.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reveal the reasoning, heuristics, or prior dead-ends that lead to a definition or idea; present alternatives or failed attempts if useful to show why the successful choice is natural.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural development: trace plausible thought processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rather than presenting only polished finished arguments, exposition should trace plausible thought processes that lead naturally to the key insight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize material to emulate a believable pathway of discovery (not necessarily the author's actual path), thereby making the emergence of the insight feel inevitable; avoid presenting the result as if it fell fully formed from nowhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make proofs feel inevitable; avoid 'magic-trick' proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: A good exposition makes the proof feel inevitable in retrospect — the reader feels they could have done it themselves. The opposite is the 'magic-trick' proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate exposition by whether it converts surprise into plausibility: if the reader, after reading, perceives the argument as the natural solution, the exposition succeeds; if the reader perceives cleverness without understanding, it fails.
